content: Urea is an organic compound with the chemical formula (NH2)2CO. It is also referred to as carbamide, particularly in the context of the International Nonproprietary Names (INN) system used in Europe. For instance, the medicinal compound hydroxyurea, previously known as hydroxycarbamide in British nomenclature, reflects this naming convention. Other names for urea include carbamide resin, isourea, carbonyl diamide, and carbonyl diamine. Urea holds historical significance as the first organic compound to be synthesized artificially from inorganic starting materials, a discovery that debunked the theory of vitalism. Urea was first identified by Hilaire Rouelle in 1773. In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler synthesized urea from inorganic materials by reacting potassium cyanate with ammonium sulfate. Wöhler’s work, although initially aimed at producing ammonium cyanate, inadvertently disproved the vitalism theory, which posited that chemicals in living organisms were fundamentally distinct from those in non-living matter. This breakthrough marked the beginning of organic chemistry as a scientific discipline. Wöhler famously wrote to Berzelius, stating, I must tell you that I can make urea without the use of kidneys, either man or dog. Ammonium cyanate is urea. Urea is naturally found in the urine of mammals and amphibians, as well as in some fish. Birds and reptiles, however, excrete uric acid, a nitrogen metabolism product that requires less water. Urea is highly soluble in water, making it an efficient means for the human body to excrete excess nitrogen. This solubility is due to extensive hydrogen bonding with water molecules, with up to six hydrogen bonds forming per urea molecule. These bonds include two from the oxygen atom and one from each hydrogen atom. This property also makes urea an effective fertilizer. Structurally, the urea molecule is planar and retains full molecular symmetry. Each carbonyl oxygen atom can accept four N-H-O hydrogen bonds, an unusual feature for this type of bond. The dense hydrogen bond network, while energetically favorable, results in an open molecular structure with ribbon-like formations creating square cross-section tunnels. The atoms in a urea molecule originate from carbon dioxide, water, aspartate, and ammonia through a metabolic pathway known as the urea cycle. This anabolic process requires energy expenditure because ammonia, a common metabolic waste product, is toxic and must be neutralized. Urea production occurs in the liver and is regulated by N-acetylglutamate. The urea cycle, initially called the Krebs-Henseleit cycle, was partially elucidated by Hans Adolf Krebs and Kurt Henseleit in 1932. Its details were further clarified in the 1940s with the identification of intermediates such as citrulline and argininosuccinate. In this cycle, amino groups from ammonia and L-aspartate are converted into urea, with intermediates including L-ornithine, citrulline, L-argininosuccinate, and L-arginine. Most organisms must excrete nitrogen waste derived from protein and amino acid catabolism. Aquatic organisms primarily excrete ammonia, while terrestrial organisms convert ammonia into urea or uric acid to mitigate its toxicity. Birds and saurians excrete uric acid, whereas mammals and other species excrete urea. Interestingly, tadpoles excrete ammonia but switch to urea production during metamorphosis. In veterinary medicine, Dalmatian dogs are notable for excreting uric acid in their urine instead of urea due to a genetic defect affecting the enzymes involved in the urea cycle. Despite this generalization, the urea cycle has been documented in a wide range of organisms, including birds, invertebrates, insects, plants, yeast, fungi, and microorganisms. While urea is primarily a waste product, it plays a crucial role in forming hypertonic urine. In the distal portions of the kidney's collecting duct, urea is reintroduced into the kidney medulla to increase osmolarity, facilitating water reabsorption into the body via osmosis through aquaporins. A small amount of urea is also excreted in human sweat, along with sodium chloride and water. Urea can irritate the skin and eyes. Excessively high concentrations in the blood can damage organs, while low concentrations, such as those found in urine, are not harmful. Urea runoff from fertilizers has been implicated in algal blooms that produce toxins, contributing to environmental concerns. Prolonged or repeated skin contact with urea in fertilizer form may cause dermatitis. The substance also irritates the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. When heated above its melting point, urea decomposes, releasing toxic gases. It reacts violently with strong oxidants, nitrites, inorganic chlorides, chlorites, and perchlorates, posing fire and explosion hazards. In laboratory settings, urea is a potent protein denaturant, used to increase the solubility of certain proteins at concentrations up to 10 M. It disrupts noncovalent bonds in proteins and is also a precursor in the synthesis of urea nitrate, a high explosive similar to ammonium nitrate but potentially more powerful due to its complexity, with a velocity of detonation (VOD) ranging from 11,000 to 15,420 feet per second. Medically, urea is used in topical dermatological products to promote skin rehydration. When applied under an occlusive dressing, 40% urea preparations can be used for non-surgical debridement of nails. Urea is also a key component in the blood urea nitrogen (BUN) test, a common marker of renal function. Isotopically labeled urea (using carbon-14 or carbon-13) is employed in the urea breath test to detect Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium found in the stomach and duodenum. This test identifies the urease enzyme produced by H. pylori, which converts urea into ammonia, raising the pH of the surrounding stomach environment. Similar bacteria in animals, such as apes, dogs, and cats, can also be identified using this test. Ureas, or carbamides, are a class of chemical compounds characterized by the functional group R(R')N-CO-N(R)(R'), which consists of a carbonyl group flanked by two organic amine residues. These compounds can be synthesized in the laboratory by reacting phosgene with primary or secondary amines. Examples of ureas include carbamide peroxide, allantoin, and hydantoin. Ureas are closely related to biurets and structurally similar to amides, carbamates, diimides, carbodiimides, and thiocarbamides. Urea reacts with alcohols to form urethanes and with malonic esters to produce barbituric acids.
